Main Group A rotavirus (RV) is the most common cause of moderate-to-severe diarrhoea in children aged < 2 years-old1. An estimated 128,000 deaths in children under 5 years were caused by RV in 2023, over 100,000 of which occurred in sub-Saharan Africa2. Inclusion of RV vaccines in immunisation schedules has contributed to a reduction in RV gastroenteritis (RVGE) disease, hospitalisation and death3–5. Early trials of RV vaccination in high-income settings uniformly demonstrated high levels of vaccine efficacy (> 90%)6. However, in low-income settings, including in sub-Saharan Africa, vaccine effectiveness has been found to be as low as 38%7,8. Improving RV vaccine efficacy in African populations will require a robust understanding of the aetiology of disparate vaccine efficacy between high and low-income settings. Causes of this disparity are likely to be multifactorial, with force of infection, strain diversity, breastfeeding, malnutrition, environmental enteropathy and host genetics all hypothesised to contribute9. Rotaviruses are double-stranded RNA viruses. The RV genome consists of 11 segments that encode 6 structural proteins (VP1, VP2, VP3, VP4, VP6 and VP7) and 6 non-structural proteins (NSP1-6). Variation in one of these structural proteins, VP6 gives rise to 10 RV species (A-J), of which group A RVs (GARV) cause over 90% of human infection. Within GARVs, strain diversity is defined by sequence variation at the two segments encoding the outer layer structural proteins: VP7 encodes the glycoprotein (G), and VP4 encodes a protease-sensitive spike protein (P)10. Some RV strains, dependent on P genotype, have been shown to use A-type human blood group antigen (HBGA) as an attachment factor11. The presence of HBGA on mucosal surfaces is mediated by the alpha (1,2) fucosyltransferase enzyme encoded by FUT2, and homozygous carriers of a common FUT2 nonsense mutation (rs601338:A) are termed non-secretors, and do not express HBGA on mucosal surfaces or secrete them in bodily fluids12. Moreover, another fucosyltransferase, encoded by FUT3, determines fucosylation of HBGA precursor glycans defining Lewis antigen status, which is also associated with RV binding affinity in vitro13. Identity and location of HBGA can thus determine likelihood of rotavirus attachment, invasion, disease and subsequent immunity in a P genotype-dependent manner. Candidate gene studies have established host genetic variation as a major determinant of RV disease and immunity. These studies have focussed on the role of HBGA in RV disease risk and immune responses. In keeping with studies defining binding affinities of RV P antigen, these data have determined reproducible effects of FUT2 genotype (secretor status) on RV disease risk in vaccinated and unvaccinated children: non-secretors are protected against P[4] and P[8] RV strains but not P[6] genotypes14–22. Moreover, the FUT3 locus, determining Lewis antigen expression, is also a determinant of RV disease risk, with Lewis negative individuals protected against P[4] and P[8] genotype disease but at increased risk of P[6] disease14–19,21. Despite the demonstration of epistasis between the FUT2 locus and ABO blood group in other contexts23, ABO blood group has not been found to be consistently associated with RV disease risk15–17,19,21,24. Secretor status has been shown to associate with naturally-acquired anti-RV antibody responses (serum IgG, neutralising antibody titres and salivary IgA) in adults13,15,25,26, but has been inconsistently associated with vaccine responses as have Lewis antigen expression and ABO blood group17,27–31. That the effects of secretor status on vaccine response are variable may reflect confounding by immune responses to natural infection, especially in settings where RV infection remains common despite immunisation. Live attenuated anti-RV vaccines contain P[8] genotype virus and are administered orally. Where an association between RV vaccine response and secretor status is observed, the direction of effect is one in which individuals protected against P[8] disease (non-secretors) have poor vaccine responses, suggesting a model where non-secretors fail to support vaccine attachment and replication preventing generation of robust immune responses. Candidate gene studies of HBGA expression and identity have thus defined a role for host genetics in RV disease risk and immunity. They do not, however, explain the poor RV vaccine efficacy in African populations. Non-secretor allele frequencies are comparable in African and European populations (minor allele frequency – MAF-Africa = 0.50, MAF-Europe = 0.47; https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), and while Lewis negative individuals are more common in African populations, P[6] genotype vaccine failures among non-secretor, Lewis negative individuals make, at most, a modest contribution to observed vaccine failure17. Serum anti-RV IgA levels are associated with protection against RV infection in vaccinated32 and unvaccinated33 individuals. A protective threshold of > 20IU/ml has been proposed as a correlate of protection against RVGE in vaccinated infants34, however, the generalizability of this threshold across settings is unclear35. In settings where RV immunisation lacks high effectiveness, anti-RV IgA will accrue following vaccination but also following RV infection. Naturally-acquired anti-RV immunity is thus likely to confound the interpretation of anti-RV IgA levels in settings with poor vaccine performance. In keeping with RV disease risk and vaccine take, the acquisition of anti-RV IgA following RV infection is likely to be under genetic control, however the contribution of host genetic variation to this, and its interaction with disease risk, is undefined. Page 3/19 Unbiased assessments of host genetics, e.g. genome-wide association studies (GWAS), are preferable to candidate gene studies, in that they do not rely on prior biological knowledge, and allow more complete estimates of the contribution of host genetics to a given trait. To date, there are no published GWAS of RV disease or immunity. We address this in this study, performing GWAS of both hospitalised RVGE in Kenyan children and anti-RV-specific IgA levels in Ugandan children, replicating our findings for RV immunity in Zambian infants and for diarrhoeal disease risk in Ugandan children (Fig. 1a). In doing so, we confirm the role of secretor status as a major genetic determinant of RV disease and immunity, define its interaction with Lewis antigen and ABO blood group, and identify genetic regulation of LIMS1 expression and hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) secretion in monocytes as a novel determinant of both traits. Results RV immunity in Ugandan children Serum anti-RV IgA quantification passed quality control thresholds in 616 Ugandan children aged 2 (n = 330) and 3 years (n = 286). At the age of 2–3 years, Ugandan children recruited to the Entebbe Mother and Baby Study (EMaBS) had median anti-RV IgA levels of 105 IU/ml, with an overall seroprevalence (anti- RV IgA ≥ 20 IU/ml) of 76% (Fig. 1b). Anti-RV IgA levels increased with age (Wilcoxon rank sum P = 0.049), with median levels at 2 years of 83 IU/ml, rising to 117 IU/ml at the age of 3 years (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). Similarly, the proportion of seropositive children also increased with age at sampling (72% aged 2 years, 82% aged 3 years, P = 2.6x10− 3). Female participants had higher anti-RV IgA levels (male median anti-RV IgA = 82 IU/ml, female median anti-RV IgA = 124 IU/ml, Wilcoxon rank sum P = 0.014), although sex was not associated with seropositivity (79% male, 76% female). In keeping with the importance of rotavirus as a cause of infant diarrhoea in this population, increased episodes of diarrhoea in the first year of life are associated with raised serum anti-RV IgA at 2–3 years in Ugandan children (ordinal regression P = 0.004). RV disease in Kenyan children Of 554 children admitted with RV disease recruited to the study, 448 had complete G and P genotype data. Of these, 407 children had a single defined RV genotype (Supplementary Table 2), with 41 mixed genotype infections (9%). As we have previously reported36, the majority of RV were genotypes G1P[8] (n = 208, 46%), G9P[8] (n = 62, 14%), G8P[4] (n = 49, 11%), G8P[6] (n = 23, 5%) and G2P[4] (n = 18, 4%). In total, there were 333 P[8] genotype infections, 47 P[6] and 92 P[4]. Children hospitalised with RV disease had a median age of 10 months (range 0-133) and 225 (41%) were female (Fig. 1d). Age and sex were not predictive of P genotype of RV disease. The majority of children presented with diarrhoea (n = 514, 97%), vomiting (n = 463, 87%) and fever (n = 408, 77%). Children presented with clinical features of hypovolaemic shock in 135 cases (25%) and 8 children died (2%). The median duration of hospital stay was 4 days (range 0–40). Among children hospitalised with RV disease in this population, P genotype, age or sex were not significant modifiers of clinical presentation or course (Supplementary Table 3), although diarrhoea was less prominent as a presenting symptom in older children. GWAS of RV immunity & disease Following SNP and sample QC, genotypes at 16,394,501 autosomal SNPs from 611 samples were included in the GWAS of anti-RV-specific serum IgA levels in Ugandan children. The genomic inflation factor (λ = 1.00) and inspection of the QQ-plot (Supplementary Fig. 2a) are not suggestive of uncontrolled confounding variation. Genome-wide association analysis revealed two loci associated with RV immunity at genome-wide significance (Fig. 1c, Table 1). The first of these loci, rs601338:A, located in FUT2 on chromosome 19 (P = 1.46x10− 15, β=-0.42), determines secretor status, which is well described as a major genetic determinant of RV infection traits14–22. The second associated locus, rs59241810:T, located on chromosome 2q12 (P = 1.65x10− 12, β = 0.56), has not previously been identified as a determinant of RV disease or immunity. The funder had no role OPINION From climate hazards to early warning: Salmonella as a sentinel for the Climate–AMR– WASH nexus Li Tang1☯, Lin Teng1☯, Min Yue 1,2* 1 Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou, China, 2 Department of Infectious Diseases, Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, China ☯ These authors contributed equally to this work. * myue@ucas.ac.cn Climate change, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), persistent deficits in water, sanita­ tion, and hygiene (WASH), and inadequate waste management are often managed as separate public-health priorities. In practice, they converge across catchments, food systems, sanitation networks, wastewater streams, and climate-vulnerable com­ munities. Floods can overwhelm sanitation and redistribute human and animal faecal contamination; drought can concentrate pathogens in scarce water; and heat can alter pathogen persistence, exposure, and antimicrobial selection [1,2]. Yet clinical, food-safety, veterinary, wastewater, and drinking-water programmes remain frag­ mented, delaying recognition of coupled ecological and microbial risks until outbreaks or resistant infections emerge. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) 2026 Guidelines for drinking-water quality recommend preventive, risk-based management from catchment to consumer [3]. The WHO water, sanitation, hygiene and waste strategy 2026–2035 reports that unsafe WASH causes at least 1.4 million preventable deaths annually and that 2.1 billion people lack safely managed drinking water [4]. It also calls for stronger regu­ latory and monitoring systems. Global genomic evidence further associates climate change with an estimated 10% rise in antimicrobial-resistance gene abundance in Salmonella [5]. Together, these findings expose an operational gap: health systems lack a practical biological signal that can connect climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging resistance early enough to support prevention. We argue that Salmonella enterica, encompassing typhoidal and non-typhoidal pathogens, is a strong candidate for such a climate sentinel. It is clinically conse­ quential when comparing with the model organism Escherichia coli, spans human, animal, food, water, and environmental compartments, and is already captured by several surveillance systems [5–8]. We therefore propose the Salmonella-Integrated Climate-Resilient WASH framework (SICREW) to connect these existing signals with climate triggers and predefined public-health responses. PLOS Climate | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0001040 August 21, 2026 2 / 4 The strategic imperative for sentinel pathogens in planetary health Pathogen-by-pathogen monitoring is impractical across the broad, dynamic, and infrastructure-dependent WASH disease landscape. WHO identifies more than 50 organisms transmitted through inadequate WASH and highlights ten that contribute substantially to the burden: pathogenic Escherichia coli, Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella spp., Shigella, Campylobacter, rotavirus, norovirus, hepatitis A virus, adenovirus, and Cryptosporidium [6]. This diversity creates a signal-to-noise problem. Surveil­ lance must identify organisms that not only document contamination but also provide actionable information about system failure. A useful sentinel pathogen must therefore do more than appear on a priority list. It must connect biological plausibility with operational value. Specifically, it should circulate across the compartments where risks arise; remain detectable under environ­ mentally variable conditions; respond to sanitation failure, hydrological extremes, and antimicrobial selection; carry interpretable genomic and AMR signals; and be measur­ able using tools that are scalable beyond highly resourced laboratories. Among major WASH-related pathogens, Salmonella meets these requirements unusually well [5–7]. Why Salmonella is a promising sentinel: Five core advantages 1. One Health connectivity. Non-typhoidal Salmonella circulates among livestock, wildlife, food, water, and people. Human-adapted S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi more specifically signal human faecal contamination and unsafe water. Together, they provide a dual lens on zoonotic connectivity and sanitation failure [6–8]. 2. Environmental resilience. Salmonella persists in water, soil, sediment, plant surfaces, and food-production environments, and its survival responds to condi­ tions disrupted by heat, floods, and drought [9]. In a study of 488,232 genomes, climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance were estimated in 82 of 100 countries evaluated [5]. 3. Genomic plasticity. Mobile genetic elements structure the Salmonella resistome. Whole-genome sequencing can therefore help distinguish clonal expansion, repeated introduction, and resistance dissemination, rather than merely record presence or absence [10]. 4. WASH actionability. Detection can indicate failures in source protection, treat­ ment, distribution integrity, sanitation containment, irrigation-water quality, or animal-waste management. WHO’s identification of Salmonella as a priority WASH-related pathogen supports its use as a context-specific verification signal within risk-based water safety management [3,6]. 5. Clinical relevance and scalability. WHO classifies fluoroquinolone-resistant S. Typhi and non-typhoidal Salmonella as high-priority bacterial pathogens [11]. Typhoidal and invasive non-typhoidal disease remain clinically important, espe­ cially in vulnerable populations [12]. Culture and antimicrobial-susceptibility testing are widely established, while referral-based sequencing can add source attribution and transmission tracking [13]. in the decision to submit the manuscript for publication. Competing interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist. PLOS Climate | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0001040 August 21, 2026 3 / 4 Salmonella should complement, not replace, faecal indicators, sanitary inspection, and pathogen-specific monitoring. No single organism captures every WASH failure or the behaviour of viruses and disinfectant-resistant protozoa. The proposed SICREW framework: From climate signal to preventive action SICREW is a four-tier pathway aligned with WHO’s risk-based, catchment-to-consumer approach [3,4]. It links climate warnings to locally interpretable biological signals and predefined public-health responses, as summarized in Table 1, thereby operationalising calls to address climate change and AMR as interconnected issues [14]. SICREW would shift Salmonella surveillance from retrospective detection toward anticipatory public health intelli­ gence. This shift is especially relevant for low- and middle-income countries, where broad multiplex pathogen testing may remain financially or technically unrealistic, but Salmonella culture, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and referral-based sequencing can be built through existing clinical, food safety, and public health laboratory networks, which can also benefit Global Health, including high-income countries. Implementation priorities for planetary health Moving SICREW into practice requires four commitments. First, climate triggers and response protocols should be incor­ porated into climate-resilient water safety planning. Pilots should predefine sampling triggers, measure warning lead time, quantify false alerts, and test whether sentinel signals change WASH or AMR decisions. Second, demonstration proj­ ects should focus on climate-vulnerable settings with high enteric-disease burdens, rapid urbanisation, weak sanitation infrastructure, and established or emerging One Health AMR networks. Third, investment should build local capacity in culture, antimicrobial-susceptibility testing, sequencing, bioinformatics, interpretation, and decision-making. Data-sharing arrangements should protect community interests, return actionable results to participating countries, and avoid extractive surveillance. Infrastructural, institutional, and social barriers can otherwise undermine environmental AMR surveillance in low- and middle-income settings [15]. Fourth, utilities and ministries should specify intervention thresholds, responsi­ ble actors, financing, and evaluation criteria before thresholds are crossed. This emphasis on accountable, multisectoral implementation is consistent with WHO’s WASH strategy [4]. The evidence base should advance alongside implementation. Priorities include quantifying climate–Salmonella–AMR dose–response relationships and establishing site-specific baselines. Studies should also compare sentinel and syn­ dromic surveillance, evaluate the added value of wastewater and environmental sampling, and test how signals can guide WASH investment, vaccination, food-chain controls, and antimicrobial stewardship [14]. SICREW should be judged by predictive lead time, decision usefulness, cost-effectiveness, and equitable prevention, not by sample volume or dash­ board production. Table 1. The SICREW framework: operational tiers for sentinel-driven surveillance. Tier Core function Operational value Baseline sentinel integration Embed routine Salmonella culture, antimicrobial-susceptibility testing, and targeted sequencing within clinical, food-safety, veterinary, drinking-water, and wastewater surveillance. Establish local baselines for occurrence, resistance, and genomic relatedness. Climate-triggered intensification Increase sampling after extreme rainfall, flooding, heatwaves, drought, and inter­ mittent or low-pressure water supply. Test whether climate warnings precede contamination or resistance enrichment. One Health data fusion Link biological signals with meteorological, hydrological, WASH, antimicrobial-use, and epidemiological data using transparent models. Identify hotspots and transmission bridges while reporting uncertainty and data gaps. Policy feedback Convert results into risk maps and locally validated intervention thresholds for utilities, laboratories, ministries, and communities. Trigger source protection, sanitation repair, food-chain controls, vaccination, and antimicrobial stewardship. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0001040.t001 PLOS Climate | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pclm.0001040 August 21, 2026 4 / 4 Conclusion: From sentinel to protective action Climate change is reshaping the environmental conditions under which enteric pathogens persist, move, and acquire resistance. Salmonella offers a practical, complementary sentinel for the climate–AMR–WASH nexus because it connects human disease, animal reservoirs, environmental persistence, genomic change, AMR emergence, and WASH-system performance. SICREW provides a pathway for translating that biological signal into preventive action by integrating climate intelligence, water safety planning, One Health surveillance, and policy feedback. Its utility must be locally vali­ dated and governed equitably; nevertheless, it offers a concrete, neat route from fragmented monitoring towards earlier, climate-resilient protection. title_original: From climate hazards to early warning: Salmonella as a sentinel for the Climate–AMR–WASH nexus

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the lack of practical biological signals linking climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to support early prevention.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed global genomic evidence from 488,232 Salmonella genomes across 100 countries to estimate climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance.
analysis.methods: Whole-genome sequencing was used to distinguish clonal expansion, repeated introduction, and resistance dissemination, while culture and antimicrobial-susceptibility testing were employed for source attribution and transmission tracking.
analysis.main_results: Climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance were estimated in 82 of 100 countries evaluated based on global genomic evidence.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight an operational gap in health systems, as they lack a practical biological signal to connect climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging resistance early enough for prevention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that Salmonella can serve as a sentinel pathogen to inform WASH interventions and AMR monitoring, offering a practical tool for early warning systems.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on global genomic evidence and does not provide detailed statistical analyses or specific sample size information, which limits the confidence in the exact magnitude of the observed effects.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of Salmonella as a sentinel pathogen for the Climate–AMR–WASH nexus, highlighting the need for a practical biological signal to connect climate hazards, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) disruptions with emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR). By analyzing global genomic evidence from 488,232 Salmonella genomes across 100 countries, the research estimates climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance. The findings suggest that Salmonella can complement existing surveillance systems and provide early warning for WASH and AMR interventions. However, the study's reliance on genomic data without detailed statistical analysis limits the confidence in its conclusions. The implications emphasize the importance of integrating climate intelligence, water safety planning, and One Health surveillance to develop effective early warning systems, while also addressing infrastructural and institutional barriers in low- and middle-income countries.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究分析了来自 100 个国家共计 488,232 株沙门菌 基因组 的全球基因组证据,以估计耐药基因丰度与气候因素相关的增长。
elements_zh.methods: 采用全基因组测序区分克隆扩散、重复输入及耐药传播;同时通过培养及抗生素药敏试验进行溯源归因与 传播 追踪。
elements_zh.main_results: 基于全球基因组证据,在所评估的 100 个国家中,有 82 个国家的耐药基因丰度呈现出与气候相关的增长。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果揭示了卫生系统的一个操作性缺口:缺乏可实际应用的生物学信号,无法及时将气候灾害、环境卫生(WASH)中断与新发耐药性联系起来,从而支持预防工作。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,沙门菌可作为哨点病原体,为环境卫生干预及耐药性监测提供信息,为早期预警系统提供实用工具。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究基于全球基因组证据,未提供详细统计分析或具体样本量信息,限制了所观察效应的确切幅度的置信度。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the lack of practical biological signals linking climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to support early prevention.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed global genomic evidence from 488,232 Salmonella genomes across 100 countries to estimate climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance.
analysis_en.methods: Whole-genome sequencing was used to distinguish clonal expansion, repeated introduction, and resistance dissemination, while culture and antimicrobial-susceptibility testing were employed for source attribution and transmission tracking.
analysis_en.main_results: Climate-associated increases in AMR-gene abundance were estimated in 82 of 100 countries evaluated based on global genomic evidence.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight an operational gap in health systems, as they lack a practical biological signal to connect climate hazards, WASH disruption, and emerging resistance early enough for prevention.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that Salmonella can serve as a sentinel pathogen to inform WASH interventions and AMR monitoring, offering a practical tool for early warning systems.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on global genomic evidence and does not provide detailed statistical analyses or specific sample size information, which limits the confidence in the exact magnitude of the observed effects.

title: A contamination-free lateral flow platform for point-of-care virus detection in wastewater

source_records.title: A contamination-free lateral flow platform for point-of-care virus detection in wastewater

priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
full_text: Abstract Wastewater-based surveillance is a recent, innovative strategy for tracking enteric virus circulation, thus providing early warning of infectious disease outbreaks. However, actual wastewater monitoring is limited by the lack of rapid, portable, and contamination-resistant molecular assays suitable for decentralized applications. Preventing amplicon aerosol contamination while maintaining high analytical sensitivity remains also a major challenge for nucleic acid detection based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) in environmental samples. We developed a fully closed recombinase polymerase amplification combined with CRISPR-associated protein 13a lateral flow assay for contamination-free detection of norovirus and rotavirus in wastewater. The platform was evaluated using synthetic ribonucleic acid standards and validated with 28 wastewater samples collected from a municipal wastewater treatment plant in China over 12 months, with each sample analyzed for both viruses. The closed reaction system integrated isothermal amplification, the collateral cleavage activity of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated protein 13a, and gold nanoparticle-based lateral flow detection within a sealed reaction vessel. Performance was assessed by analytical sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Results show that the optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 1 attomolar in approximately 90 min, showed no cross-reactivity with tested non-target viruses. Analysis of the two target viruses in 28 wastewater samples generated 56 virus-specific test results, with 14 positive detections, comparable to quantitative polymerase chain reaction. These findings demonstrate ultrasensitive, contamination-free virus detection and provide a portable platform for wastewater-based epidemiology and on-site public health surveillance. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Wastewater-based surveillance is a recent, innovative strategy for tracking enteric virus circulation, thus providing early warning of infectious disease outbreaks. However, actual wastewater monitoring is limited by the lack of rapid, portable, and contamination-resistant molecular assays suitable for decentralized applications. Preventing amplicon aerosol contamination while maintaining high analytical sensitivity remains also a major challenge for nucleic acid detection based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) in environmental samples. We developed a fully closed recombinase polymerase amplification combined with CRISPR-associated protein 13a lateral flow assay for contamination-free detection of norovirus and rotavirus in wastewater. The platform was evaluated using synthetic ribonucleic acid standards and validated with 28 wastewater samples collected from a municipal wastewater treatment plant in China over 12 months, with each sample analyzed for both viruses. The closed reaction system integrated isothermal amplification, the collateral cleavage activity of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats-associated protein 13a, and gold nanoparticle-based lateral flow detection within a sealed reaction vessel. Performance was assessed by analytical sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Results show that the optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 1 attomolar in approximately 90 min, showed no cross-reactivity with tested non-target viruses. Analysis of the two target viruses in 28 wastewater samples generated 56 virus-specific test results, with 14 positive detections, comparable to quantitative polymerase chain reaction. These findings demonstrate ultrasensitive, contamination-free virus detection and provide a portable platform for wastewater-based epidemiology and on-site public health surveillance. title_original: A contamination-free lateral flow platform for point-of-care virus detection in wastewater

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of current wastewater monitoring by developing a contamination-free detection platform for norovirus and rotavirus, which are key enteric viruses of public health concern. The background highlights the need for rapid, portable, and contamination-resistant molecular assays for decentralized wastewater-based surveillance.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and validation of a closed reaction system for detecting norovirus and rotavirus in wastewater samples collected from a municipal treatment plant in China over 12 months. The platform was tested on 28 wastewater samples, with each sample analyzed for both target viruses.
analysis.methods: The platform utilized recombinase polymerase amplification combined with CRISPR-associated protein 13a lateral flow assay. Performance was evaluated through analytical sensitivity, specificity, and agreement with quantitative polymerase chain reaction.
analysis.main_results: The optimized assay achieved a limit of detection of 1 attomolar in approximately 90 minutes and showed no cross-reactivity with tested non-target viruses. Analysis of the two target viruses in 28 wastewater samples generated 56 virus-specific test results, with 14 positive detections.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate the platform's ability to provide ultrasensitive, contamination-free virus detection, which is a novel approach for wastewater-based epidemiology and on-site public health surveillance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The platform offers a portable solution for wastewater-based surveillance, which can enhance early warning systems for infectious disease outbreaks and support real-time public health monitoring.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is limited to synthetic RNA standards and 28 wastewater samples, which may affect generalizability. However, the results are consistent with quantitative polymerase chain reaction, suggesting moderate confidence in the platform's performance.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a contamination-free lateral flow platform for detecting norovirus and rotavirus in wastewater. The platform combines recombinase polymerase amplification with CRISPR-associated protein 13a and gold nanoparticle-based detection. It was validated using synthetic RNA standards and 28 wastewater samples from a Chinese treatment plant over 12 months, achieving a limit of detection of 1 attomolar in about 90 minutes. The results showed no cross-reactivity with non-target viruses and 14 positive detections across 56 tests, comparable to quantitative polymerase chain reaction. The findings highlight the platform's potential for enhancing wastewater-based epidemiology and public health surveillance. However, the study's limited sample size and reliance on synthetic standards may affect generalizability, resulting in moderate confidence in the results.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在通过开发一种无污染检测平台,解决当前废水监测的局限性,该平台针对轮状病毒和另一种肠道病毒(轮状病毒为公共卫生关注的关键肠道病毒)。背景强调了对适用于分散废水基监测的快速、便携且抗污染分子检测方法的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究开发并验证了一种封闭反应系统,用于在中国某市政污水处理厂收集的废水样本中检测轮状病毒和另一种肠道病毒,收集期为12个月。该平台在28份废水样本上进行了测试,每份样本均检测两种靶标病毒。
elements_zh.methods: 该平台采用重组聚合酶扩增与CRISPR相关蛋白13a侧向流检测技术。通过分析灵敏度、特异性及与定量聚合酶链反应(qPCR)的符合性评估其性能。
elements_zh.main_results: 优化后的检测方法在约90分钟内实现了1阿托摩尔的检测限,且与测试的非靶标病毒无交叉反应。在28份废水样本中对两种靶标病毒进行分析,共产生56个病毒特异性检测结果,其中14个为阳性检测。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果证明该平台具备超灵敏、无污染的病毒检测能力,这是废水基监测和现场公共卫生监测的一种新颖方法。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该平台为废水基监测提供便携式解决方案,可增强传染病预警系统,并支持实时公共卫生监测。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的证据仅限于合成RNA标准品和28份废水样本,可能影响结果的普遍性。然而,结果与定量聚合酶链反应(qPCR)一致,表明该平台性能具有中等可信度。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在通过开发一种无污染检测平台,解决当前废水监测的局限性,该平台针对轮状病毒和另一种肠道病毒(轮状病毒为公共卫生关注的关键肠道病毒)。背景强调了对适用于分散废水基监测的快速、便携且抗污染分子检测方法的需求。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究开发并验证了一种封闭反应系统,用于在中国某市政污水处理厂收集的废水样本中检测轮状病毒和另一种肠道病毒,收集期为12个月。该平台在28份废水样本上进行了测试,每份样本均检测两种靶标病毒。
analysis_zh.methods: 该平台采用重组聚合酶扩增与CRISPR相关蛋白13a侧向流检测技术。通过分析灵敏度、特异性及与定量聚合酶链反应(qPCR)的符合性评估其性能。
analysis_zh.main_results: 优化后的检测方法在约90分钟内实现了1阿托摩尔的检测限,且与测试的非靶标病毒无交叉反应。在28份废水样本中对两种靶标病毒进行分析,共产生56个病毒特异性检测结果,其中14个为阳性检测。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果证明该平台具备超灵敏、无污染的病毒检测能力,这是废水基监测和现场公共卫生监测的一种新颖方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该平台为废水基监测提供便携式解决方案,可增强传染病预警系统,并支持实时公共卫生监测。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的证据仅限于合成RNA标准品和28份废水样本,可能影响结果的普遍性。然而,结果与定量聚合酶链反应(qPCR)一致,表明该平台性能具有中等可信度。
